To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we identified the homologues of the C2 neuron in four species of nudibranch molluscs using a combination of neuroanatomical and neurochemical criteria.
we used neurochemical and neuroanatomical markers to identify C2 in four species of nudibranchs that do not display the type of swimming behaviors exhibited by Tritonia and Pleurobranchaea.
neurochemical markers and previously known neuroanatomy allowed the identification of a neuron that is a member of the Tritonia swim CPG.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural basis of behavior.
identifying the homologue of a neuron that is a member of a central pattern generator.
the neural mechanisms underlying behavior, specifically the identification of neurons involved in swimming behavior across species of molluscs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
C2 can be identified by a combination of neurochemical and neuroanatomical features that are conserved across species, and that are independent of behavioral function.
neurochemical and neuroanatomical properties can be used to identify homologous neurons in species that do not display the behavior that was used to initially describe those neurons.
the C2 neuron in Tritonia diomedae is the homologue of the A1 neuron in Pleurobranchae californica and the C2 homolog in Melibe leionina, Hermissena crassicornis and Flabellena iodinea.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
neuroanatomical and neurochemical features can be used to identify homologous neurons that are members of a CPG, even in species that lack the behavior that the neuron is known to control.

the neurochemical and neuroanatomical properties of C2 can be used across species to identify the C2 homolog in species that do not display the behavior that is typically associated with the C2 neuron.
the C2 neuron is the first identified homologous neuron across the Nudipleurans, which is a large and ecologically important clade within Opisthobranchia.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in some cases, neurochemical and neuroanatomical properties can be used to identify homologous neurons without relying on behavioral or physiological characteristics.

the neuroanatomical and neurochemical markers used to identify CPG neuron homologues in the Nudipleuran molluscs Tritonia diomedaea and Pleurobranchaea can be applied across species, even when species-specific behaviors are not present.
, for species that do not display a behavior, it is still possible to identify homologous neurons by using neurochemical markers in conjunction with previously described anatomical characteristics.
